plan: SAT R&W batch 63: 10 new items on new passages CLD-P-SAT-RW-000562..000571 (Bashō and Sora WIC, bowerbird forced-perspective inference, urban heat-island quantitative evidence, Great Zimbabwe cross-text, Mansa Musa purpose, Sor Juana punctuation, Phillis Wheatley finite verb, Tarim Basin transition, Ishango bone synthesis, Chauvet inference). Topics checked against every bank and the combined bank. Difficulty provisional.

passages.title: A shaped journey
passages.text: Matsuo Bashō's The Narrow Road to the Deep North, which recounts a journey he made in 1689, has long been read as a travel diary. Yet the book is in places ______: a diary kept by Sora, the companion who walked beside him, shows that Bashō changed dates, rearranged stops, and described at least one episode that Sora never mentions.

passages.title: Building an illusion
passages.text: Male great bowerbirds build an avenue of sticks and decorate the court at its entrance with stones, bones, and shells. Researchers found that the objects are arranged so that they get larger with distance from the avenue, which can make the court look shorter to a female standing inside. When the researchers reversed the arrangement, placing large objects close and small ones far away, the males restored the original size gradient within a few days. This finding suggests that ______

passages.title: Warmer nights
passages.text:
A student measured air temperatures at a downtown site and at a farm 20 kilometers away on the same summer day.
Afternoon: downtown 31.0°C, farm 30.2°C
Night: downtown 22.5°C, farm 19.1°C
The student claims that the city's warming effect was much stronger at night than during the afternoon.

passages.title: Who built the walls
passages.text:
Text 1
In the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, several European writers who visited Great Zimbabwe, a complex of massive stone walls in southern Africa, insisted that it must have been built by foreign settlers from the Mediterranean or the Middle East.

Text 2
In 1929, archaeologist Gertrude Caton-Thompson excavated at Great Zimbabwe. She found that the pottery, tools, and other objects in the oldest layers matched those made by local African communities and that nothing in them pointed to builders from elsewhere. She concluded that the site was built by the region's own inhabitants.

passages.title: A journey remembered
passages.text: In 1324, Mansa Musa, ruler of the Mali Empire, passed through Cairo on his pilgrimage to Mecca. His entourage spent and gave away so much gold that, according to the historian al-Umari, who visited Cairo about a dozen years later, the metal's value there had still not recovered. Accounts like al-Umari's spread Mali's reputation for wealth across North Africa and into Europe, where a 1375 Catalan atlas shows Mansa Musa holding a large piece of gold.

passages.title: A defense of learning
passages.text: In 1691, the Mexican poet and scholar Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz responded to a bishop who had urged her to give up secular study. Her most famous prose work, the "Reply to Sister Philothea______ defended the right of women to pursue knowledge.

passages.title: A first poem
passages.text: Phillis Wheatley, who had been brought to Boston as an enslaved child in 1761, ______ her first poem in a Rhode Island newspaper in 1767, when she was about thirteen years old.

passages.title: Local, not migrant
passages.text: For decades, the naturally preserved bodies found in China's Tarim Basin puzzled researchers. Because the people had been buried with woolen clothing, wheat, and cheese, some proposed that they were migrants from far to the west. ______ a 2021 genetic study found that they descended from a long-isolated local population; their farming and herding practices had apparently spread to them without a large migration.

passages.title: Notes on a notched bone
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- The Ishango bone was found in 1950 near the Semliki River in what is now the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
- It is about 20,000 years old.
- It bears three columns of notches cut into its surface.
- Some researchers think the notches record counting or arithmetic.
- Others argue that they are simply a tally or decoration.

passages.title: Early mastery
passages.text: Chauvet Cave in southern France, discovered in 1994, contains paintings of lions, rhinoceroses, and horses that radiocarbon dating places at more than 30,000 years old, roughly twice the age of the paintings at Lascaux. Yet the Chauvet artists already used shading to model their animals' bodies and overlapping outlines to suggest depth. Many scholars had assumed that cave painting developed slowly from simple to sophisticated forms. The Chauvet paintings suggest instead that ______

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: Bashō changed dates, rearranged stops, and described at least one episode
candidates.explanation: Changing dates, rearranging stops, and adding an episode make parts of the book invented, or "fictionalized."

A.rationale: "Documentary" means factual, the opposite of what the comparison with Sora's diary shows.

B.rationale: Nothing suggests the book was left incomplete; the issue is accuracy.

D.rationale: Bashō is named as the author.

candidates.remember: Let the evidence after the colon define the blank.

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the gradient is something the males actively maintain.
choices.B: females prefer courts decorated with the largest objects available.
choices.C: the males cannot tell large objects from small ones.
choices.D: the illusion has no effect on how females view the court.

candidates.evidence: the males restored the original size gradient within a few days
candidates.explanation: If males quickly rebuild the gradient after it is reversed, the arrangement must be something they actively maintain.

B.rationale: The text does not say which objects females prefer.

C.rationale: Restoring the gradient shows the males do distinguish sizes.

D.rationale: The text says the arrangement can make the court look shorter.

hints: What did the males do after the reversal?

strategy.explanation: Ask what the restoration shows about the males.

candidates.remember: An inference must follow from the reported result.

candidates.stem: Which choice best uses data from the text to support the student's claim?

choices.A: Downtown was 31.0°C in the afternoon, the highest temperature recorded at either site.
choices.B: The farm cooled by 11.1°C from afternoon to night.
choices.C: Both sites were cooler at night than in the afternoon.
choices.D: Downtown was 3.4°C warmer than the farm at night but 0.8°C warmer in the afternoon.

candidates.evidence: much stronger at night than during the afternoon
candidates.explanation: The city's warming effect is the difference between the sites: 22.5 − 19.1 = 3.4°C at night and 31.0 − 30.2 = 0.8°C in the afternoon.

A.rationale: This gives one value but does not compare the city's advantage at the two times.

B.rationale: This describes the farm alone, not the difference between the sites.

C.rationale: This is true but does not show where the warming effect was stronger.

hints: How do you measure the city's warming effect?

strategy.explanation: Compute the difference between sites at each time.

candidates.remember: Support a comparison claim with the compared quantities.

candidates.stem: Based on the texts, how would Caton-Thompson (Text 2) most likely respond to the writers' claim in Text 1?

choices.A: She would agree that the walls were built by settlers but date them to a later period.
choices.B: She would say that the excavated evidence points to local builders, not foreign settlers.
choices.C: She would say that the walls are too damaged to reveal who built them.
choices.D: She would argue that the writers were right about the Mediterranean but wrong about the Middle East.

candidates.evidence: She concluded that the site was built by the region's own inhabitants
candidates.explanation: Caton-Thompson's finds matched local African material and showed no sign of foreign builders, so she would reject the writers' claim.

A.rationale: She rejected the idea of foreign builders.

C.rationale: She drew a clear conclusion from the excavated objects.

D.rationale: She found nothing pointing to builders from elsewhere.

strategy.explanation: Compare her conclusion with the claim in Text 1.

candidates.remember: Identify whether a second author supports or rejects the first.

candidates.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To describe an event and explain how it shaped outside views of Mali's wealth
choices.B: To argue that al-Umari exaggerated the amount of gold that Mansa Musa spent
choices.C: To explain how the Mali Empire obtained the gold that Mansa Musa carried
choices.D: To compare the mapmaking of North Africa with that of medieval Europe

candidates.evidence: spread Mali's reputation for wealth across North Africa and into Europe
candidates.explanation: The text recounts Mansa Musa's spending in Cairo and then traces how accounts of it spread Mali's reputation, ending with the Catalan atlas.

B.rationale: The text reports al-Umari's account without questioning it.

C.rationale: The text does not discuss where the gold came from.

D.rationale: The atlas is mentioned only as evidence of Mali's reputation.

hints: What does the last sentence add?
candidates.remember: A purpose answer should cover the whole text.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.explanation: The title is a nonessential appositive that opened with a comma after "work," so it must close with a comma before "defended"; the comma goes inside the closing quotation mark.

A.rationale: Without a comma, the nonessential title is not closed off from the verb "defended."

B.rationale: A semicolon cannot separate a subject from its verb.

D.rationale: A colon cannot come between a subject and its verb.

hints: Is the title set off by commas?

strategy.explanation: Find the comma that opens the element.

candidates.remember: A nonessential element needs punctuation on both sides.

candidates.subskill: Finite verb in a main clause
candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: Phillis Wheatley, who had been brought to Boston
candidates.explanation: The subject "Phillis Wheatley" needs a finite verb, and "published" fits the past-tense context.

A.rationale: "Publishing" is not a finite verb, so the sentence would lack a main verb.

C.rationale: "Having published" is not a finite verb, so the sentence would lack a main verb.

D.rationale: "To publish" is not a finite verb, so the sentence would lack a main verb.

hints: Does the sentence have a main verb?

strategy.explanation: Skip the clause between the commas.

candidates.remember: Every sentence needs a finite main verb.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.evidence: descended from a long-isolated local population
candidates.explanation: The genetic study overturns the earlier proposal that the people were migrants, so a contrast transition is needed.

A.rationale: The genetic study contradicts the migrant hypothesis rather than confirming it.

B.rationale: The burial goods did not cause the genetic finding.

C.rationale: The genetic finding is not similar to the migrant hypothesis.

hints: Does the study support or contradict the migrant idea?
candidates.remember: Use a contrast transition when new evidence overturns an earlier idea.

candidates.stem: The student wants to present the bone's possible significance while acknowledging that it is debated. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: The Ishango bone, found in 1950 near the Semliki River in the Congo, is about 20,000 years old.
choices.B: The three columns of notches on the Ishango bone prove that people did arithmetic 20,000 years ago.
choices.C: The Ishango bone may record early counting, though some see its notches as only a tally or decoration.
choices.D: Some researchers argue that the notches on the 20,000-year-old Ishango bone are simply a tally or decoration.

candidates.evidence: Some researchers think the notches record counting or arithmetic
candidates.explanation: Only choice C presents the possible significance (early counting) and acknowledges the opposing view.

A.rationale: This gives facts about the bone but not its possible significance or the debate.

B.rationale: "Prove" ignores the debate the student wants to acknowledge.

D.rationale: This gives only the skeptical view, not the bone's possible significance.

hints: Which choice has both the significance and the doubt?

strategy.explanation: Check each choice against both parts of the goal.

candidates.remember: A synthesis answer must address every part of the goal.

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the paintings at Lascaux were made before those at Chauvet.
choices.B: advanced techniques appeared early instead of developing slowly.
choices.C: radiocarbon dating cannot be used to determine the age of cave paintings.
choices.D: cave painters gradually abandoned shading in favor of simpler outlines.

candidates.evidence: already used shading to model their animals' bodies
candidates.explanation: Very old paintings that already use shading and overlapping outlines contradict a slow, step-by-step development, suggesting such techniques appeared early.

A.rationale: The text says Chauvet's paintings are roughly twice as old as Lascaux's.

C.rationale: The text relies on radiocarbon dates without questioning them.

D.rationale: The text does not describe any later loss of shading.

hints: What assumption do the paintings challenge?

strategy.explanation: Contrast the assumption with the finding.

candidates.remember: A finding that contradicts an assumption points to its opposite.
